content.intro: At C2, you can re-express the same underlying idea in multiple grammatical forms, shifting tone and register without changing the core meaning. This is a key skill for editing your own writing and adapting to different audiences.

rules.heading: a) Active to passive rephrasing at high nuance — beyond the basic transformation, choose active or passive deliberately based on what should be emphasized, and how formal/impersonal the text should sound.
rules.body:
Active (direct, agent-focused): The board rejected the proposal.

Passive (formal, result-focused, agent optional): The proposal was rejected (by the board). / The proposal was rejected, a decision that surprised many. (agent omitted entirely — common in formal/academic writing when the actor is unknown or unimportant)

rules.heading: b) Multiple ways to re-express the same idea with tone changes — the same content can be delivered as a blunt statement, a hedged academic claim, a formal announcement, or a rhetorical question, depending on audience and purpose.
rules.body:
Blunt: The plan failed.

Hedged/academic: It could be argued that the plan did not achieve its intended outcomes.

Formal/official: The initiative did not meet its stated objectives.

Rhetorical: Can anyone really claim that this plan succeeded?

rules.heading: c) Grammar-driven style shifts — using specific grammatical choices to signal register:
rules.body:
• Nominalization + passive = formal/academic/legal ("The implementation of the policy was delayed" vs. "They delayed implementing the policy").
  • Modal hedging (may, might, could, it would seem that) = cautious, academic tone.
  • Contractions, phrasal verbs, and direct imperatives = informal/conversational tone.
  • Cleft sentences and fronting = emphatic, persuasive, rhetorical tone. Mastering these transformations means you can take one idea and dial its formality, distance, and emphasis up or down at will.

examples: The committee approved the budget. → The budget was approved (by the committee).
They messed up the schedule badly. → The scheduling was severely mismanaged.
I think the plan won't work. → It could be argued that the plan is unlikely to succeed.
We're cutting costs next quarter. → Cost reductions will be implemented in the next quarter.
Nobody knows exactly why the project failed. → The precise cause of the project's failure remains unclear.
He clearly lied to the board. → It would appear that the information presented to the board was not entirely accurate.
Fix this now! → This issue requires immediate attention.
The team is incredibly talented. → The team's talent is beyond question.
Sales dropped a lot last quarter. → A significant decline in sales was recorded last quarter.
Everyone agrees the policy failed. → There is broad consensus that the policy did not achieve its objectives.

commonMistakes.wrong: The proposal was rejected by they.
commonMistakes.right: The proposal was rejected by them.
commonMistakes.why: After "by" in a passive sentence, use the object pronoun ("them"), not the subject pronoun.

commonMistakes.wrong: It could be argue that the plan failed.
commonMistakes.right: It could be argued that the plan failed.
commonMistakes.why: The passive hedge needs the past participle ("argued"), not the base form.

commonMistakes.wrong: The implementation of the policy delayed.
commonMistakes.right: The implementation of the policy was delayed.
commonMistakes.why: Nominalized subjects still need a full passive verb ("was delayed"), not just the past participle alone.

commonMistakes.wrong: A significant decline of sales was recorded.
commonMistakes.right: A significant decline in sales was recorded.
commonMistakes.why: "Decline" collocates with "in," not "of," when referring to a drop in a measurable quantity.

commonMistakes.wrong: There is broad consensus what the policy failed.
commonMistakes.right: There is broad consensus that the policy failed.

items.prompt: They lost a lot of money. → A substantial ___ (loss) was incurred.
items.explanation: “Substantial loss” nominalizes “lost a lot of money” into a formal noun phrase.

items.prompt: Nobody really knows why it happened. → The reason ___ remains unclear.
items.explanation: “The reason” + “why it happened”/“for this” nominalizes the vague “nobody knows why” into a formal subject.

items.prompt: I think the results are wrong. → It ___ be argued that the results are flawed.
items.explanation: “It could be argued that” is the fixed hedging frame for a personal opinion.

items.prompt: We will announce the decision tomorrow. → The decision ___ (announce) tomorrow.
items.explanation: The passive shifts focus from “we” to the decision itself, for a more formal/impersonal tone.

items.prompt: Everyone agrees this is a problem. → There is broad ___ that this is a problem.
items.explanation: “Broad consensus” nominalizes “everyone agrees” into a formal noun phrase.

items.prompt: The team messed up the launch. → The launch ___ (severely mismanage).
items.explanation: The passive shifts focus from “the team” to the launch itself, softening the blame.

exercises.title: Rewrite / Transformation
exercises.instructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite each blunt/informal sentence in a more formal, hedged, or passive register)

items.prompt: The manager screwed up the budget.
items.modelAnswer: The budget was significantly mismanaged by the manager. (or: Serious mismanagement of the budget occurred under the manager's supervision.)

items.prompt: I'm pretty sure the plan won't work.
items.modelAnswer: It could be argued that the plan is unlikely to succeed.
Job cuts will be implemented next month.

items.prompt: The report is full of mistakes.
items.modelAnswer: The report contains a considerable number of errors.

items.prompt: Nobody bothered to check the numbers.
items.modelAnswer: The figures were not adequately checked.
The website requires immediate attention, as it is currently non-functional.

items.incorrect: It could be argue that the results are inconclusive.
answer: It could be argued that the results are inconclusive.
items.explanation: The passive hedge needs the past participle (“argued”), not the base form.
A completed past action needs the past participle “announced,” not the continuous form “announcing.”

items.incorrect: There is broad consensus what needs to change.
answer: There is broad consensus about what needs to change.
items.explanation: “Consensus” is followed by “about/on,” not directly by a “what” clause.

items.incorrect: A sharp decline of revenue was reported.
answer: A sharp decline in revenue was reported.
items.explanation: “Decline” collocates with “in,” not “of,” when referring to a drop in a measurable quantity.

items.incorrect: The proposal was rejected by they.
answer: The proposal was rejected by them.
items.explanation: After “by” in a passive sentence, use the object pronoun (“them”), not the subject pronoun.

answer: The implementation was delayed for months.
items.explanation: Nominalized subjects still need a full passive verb (“was delayed”), not just the past participle alone.

exercises.title: Guided Production
exercises.instructions: Write your own sentence. There's no single correct answer — a model answer is shown for comparison after you submit.

items.prompt: Take a blunt, informal sentence you might say to a friend, and rewrite it in formal/academic register.
items.modelAnswer: Informal: "This meeting was a total waste of time." → Formal: "The meeting did not yield any substantive outcomes."

items.prompt: Write one sentence using nominalization + passive to describe a change or event (e.g., in the news, at work).
items.modelAnswer: The postponement of the launch was announced without prior notice, catching many stakeholders off guard.

items.prompt: Write one hedged academic sentence using "It could be argued that..." about a topic you have an opinion on.
items.modelAnswer: It could be argued that remote work has fundamentally changed how companies measure productivity.

items.prompt: Write the same idea twice: once as a direct statement, once as a rhetorical question with the same underlying meaning.
items.modelAnswer: Direct: "The policy failed." / Rhetorical: "Can this policy really be considered a success by any reasonable measure?"

summary: a) Active to passive rephrasing at high nuance — beyond the basic transformation, choose active or passive deliberately based on what should be emphasized, and how formal/impersonal the text should sound.

b) Multiple ways to re-express the same idea with tone changes — the same content can be delivered as a blunt statement, a hedged academic claim, a formal announcement, or a rhetorical question, depending on audience and purpose.
